blogs.title: Procedural Rights in Vacuo: The High Bar for Compelling Agency Action
blogs.description: This post explores the D.C. Circuit's rigorous application of Article III standing to procedural rights. By rejecting the idea that a 'procedural right in vacuo' is sufficient to establish a case, the court reinforces a significant hurdle for public interest groups seeking to compel government agencies to perform specific investigative functions. We will analyze how the court balances the 'relaxed' standing requirements for procedural injuries against the necessity of a concrete, particularized interest that is actually affected by the deprivation of that right.

blogs.title: The Speculative Chain: Causation and the Limits of 'Persuasive' Redressability
blogs.description: The court’s analysis of AFL's first standing theory provides a masterclass in the limitations of 'speculative' causation. The ruling clarifies that a plaintiff cannot establish standing by presenting a hypothetical chain of events involving multiple independent actors (in this case, the OSC, DOJ, and MSPB). This post will examine the court’s refusal to grant standing based on a judgment that might 'persuade' third parties, highlighting the strict requirement that a favorable decision must 'very likely spur' the specific steps necessary to redress the injury.

blogs.title: Mandatory Duties vs. Discretionary Procedures: Navigating OSC’s Enforcement Maze
blogs.description: This post examines the tension between the mandatory language of 5 U.S.C. § 1216 (which says the OSC 'shall' investigate) and the discretionary nature of the procedural steps used to conduct those investigations. By distinguishing between a legal duty to initiate an inquiry and the discretionary choice of how to manage that inquiry's progress, the court provides a roadmap for how judges handle cases involving agency enforcement discretion. We will discuss the implications for litigants trying to use the courts to micromanage agency internal processes.
